newsitem.title: USA: COBALT -- Market ponders plentiful future supplies.
newsitem.headline: COBALT -- Market ponders plentiful future supplies.

text.p: A rash of global cobalt projects is propelling that strategic metal towards oversupply, but many in the industry are crossing their fingers that some production plans fall by the wayside and higher demand mops up the extra material.

Annual worldwide output looks set to rise from 27,000 tonnes at present to 45,000 to 50,000 tonnes by the turn of the century, with most of the extra metal on stream towards the year 2000, largely as a byproduct from copper and nickel projects.

"In general the price of cobalt makes no difference to copper or nickel producers, but it may do to future ones," Michael Hawkins of trader Metals Resources Group, told the Gorham/Intertech cobalt conference in New York Wednesday.
Mark Seddon of industry analysts Roskill forecast a cobalt price of about $10 a pound, less than half the present level, around the year 2000, with a probable surplus of 5,000 tonnes.

A key factor will be the effect of lower copper prices on planned red metal projects, though consultant Peter Matheson said many of the projects in Australia - set to surge into second place in world producer pecking order - "will come about as a result of expanding nickel production."
But buoyant cobalt prices of at least $15 a pound are needed to keep some secondary cobalt projects viable, several delegates noted. This may provide a price floor, some hoped.

Repeated talk of extra supply prompted one lone delegate to suggest an OPEC type agreement for cobalt - he went unanswered. But there were several promptings for better development of markets by the "underfunded" Cobalt Development Institute.
"Pretty clearly there is gong to be some substantial cobalt resources around. The CDI nees to do even more good work and that will need funding," noted Jerry Perkins of Savage Resources.
The CDI was invited to attend the conference but declined, an organiser said.
But Mark Caffarey of cobalt processor Union Miniere, insisted there was no talk of surplus ahead. "There will be more supply, but there will also be new applications," he said.

The industry was fragmenting with many suppliers, but the intermediate sector which processes cobalt into powders and salts was rationalising itself, Caffarey said. The industry was also becoming more global, and more supply will reduce price fluctuations.
Other delegates added that stabler prices would enourage new applications and help promote existing ones.

Demand in current applications are set to grow. Dirk Naumann of H.C. Starck, forecast that the use of cobalt in consumer batteries would rise from 500 tonnes at present to between 3,000 and 5,000 tonnes by 2002, particularly if electric vehicle demand surges.
Donald Muzyka of Special Metals Corp saw western world cobalt demand for superalloys in jet engine and spare parts growing from 4,300 tonnes in 1995 to 6,900 tonnes in 2000.
Despite healthy growth in some key sectors, Roskill's Seddon said the best case scenarios indicated overall cobalt demand of 30,000 tonnes in 2000.
